name: Uneapa
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Bali-Vitu. In Lynch, Ross & Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages, 362-379. Curzon.
earlier_scan.note: Sketch of Bali (Uneapa) with phonology section

new_statements.quote: Stress is penultimate. This means that in words where Bali retains an erstwhile final consonant with a following echo vowel but Vitu loses the consonant, stress falls on different syllables in the two dialects: e.g. Bali /kau'aka/, Vitu /'kaua/ 'dog'; Bali /βo'roto/, Vitu /'βoro/ 'sun'. However, stress is most obvious in citation forms. In continuous speech, vowels tend to be of roughly equal length, suggesting that Bali-Vitu is a syllable-timed language.
new_statements.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 2002. Bali-Vitu. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds.), The Oceanic Languages (Curzon Language Family Series), 362-386. Richmond: Curzon.
new_statements.locator: p. 363, section 1.3 'Stress' (pdf page 380 of the saved book scan); variety statement p. 362
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; because Bali (Uneapa) keeps historical final consonants plus an echo vowel, the penult (and hence the stress) is one syllable later than in the Vitu cognate.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; author notes stress is clearest in citation forms and that connected speech sounds syllable-timed with vowels of roughly equal length. Sec. 1.4 notes optional clitic-final vowel loss (bali=taza -> [baltaza]) creating surface CVC syllables, without comment on stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement illustrated with citation forms; author explicitly contrasts citation forms (stress obvious) with continuous speech (less obvious). Description is of the Bali (Uneapa) dialect, data from a speaker of Ketinerave village.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 treats Bali and Vitu as two dialects of one language 'Bali-Vitu' but states (p.362) 'The description here is of Bali' (Unea Island, vernacular Uniapa = Uneapa, unea1237), with Vitu (mudu1242) mentioned only contrastively; the stress statement is therefore first-hand for Uneapa. The Vitu OPD already held under mudu1242 independently gives penultimate stress for Vitu.

sources.note: p.363 sec. 1.3 'Stress': 'Stress is penultimate.' Bali /kau'aka/ vs Vitu /'kaua/ 'dog', Bali /βo'roto/ vs Vitu /'βoro/ 'sun' (Bali keeps final C + echo vowel, so stress lands on a different syllable than in Vitu); stress most obvious in citation forms; continuous speech roughly syllable-timed. 'Stress is located at the penultimate syllable' (unsourced section; evidently from Ross 2002).
